name: Native Tongues
hook: A loose collective of New York rap groups who sampled jazz and oddball records, rapped about ideas instead of threats, and showed that rap could be playful without being a novelty.
blurb: Native Tongues started around 1988 when three groups, the Jungle Brothers, De La Soul and A Tribe Called Quest, became friends and began working together. Queen Latifah, Monie Love, Black Sheep and Chi-Ali had joined by 1989. They took the name from a line in New Birth's 'African Cry' about people whose native languages were taken from them. They were closely tied to Afrika Bambaataa's Universal Zulu Nation and are described as carrying on his spirit. Their records sampled far beyond funk breaks, into jazz, soft rock and children's educational records, and their words were about African history and pride, everyday life, looking inward, and jokes, not violence, which proved that kind of rap could sell. By 1993 the groups were drifting apart, and De La Soul's Trugoy publicly declared the movement dead. Many later rappers, including the Roots, are widely described as following their lead.
geopolitics: The groups came up in the late 1980s, when the dominant commercial stories about Black youth in American media were crack and crime. Afrocentric ideas, from Nation of Islam offshoots to the Five Percenters to the Zulu Nation, were a live part of New York rap, and Native Tongues took the gentler, more educational end of that.
whatWasNew: Jazz and soft-rock samples used as the main musical bed rather than as an occasional flourish, and rappers presenting themselves as odd, bookish or funny rather than tough, at a time when that was a commercial risk.
production: Prince Paul's production on De La Soul's '3 Feet High and Rising' (1989) and A Tribe Called Quest's in-house production by Q-Tip and Ali Shaheed Muhammad set the sound: dense sample collages and relaxed jazz loops, built on samplers of the period.
labels: Tommy Boy (De La Soul, Queen Latifah), Warner Bros. (Jungle Brothers' second album), Jive (A Tribe Called Quest) and Mercury (Black Sheep). The collective was never a label, which is part of why it came apart as each group's career pulled in its own direction.
politics: Afrocentric and anti-violence in its stated values, with lyrics about African history, community and self-respect, alongside a refusal of the gangster posture that was taking over the charts.
